problems.stem: A teacher reports: 'The app is very easy to use; even my youngest students click through it fast.' Why does this not yet establish accessibility?
options: Ease of use is the same thing as accessibility.
Usability for typical users does not show that students using screen readers, captions, or keyboard-only navigation can complete the same tasks.
Accessibility only matters for physical buildings, not software.
Fast clicking proves the tool works for everyone.
problems.explanation: Usability describes the experience of typical users. Accessibility asks whether learners who rely on assistive technology or accommodations can do the same work. The first does not demonstrate the second.

problems.stem: A vendor says the tool 'meets WCAG AA.' What evidence would let a teacher trust that claim for their classroom?
options: An accessibility conformance report (such as a VPAT) plus a check of the specific tasks students will actually perform.
The fact that the tool has many users.
A confirmation that the homepage looks accessible.
problems.explanation: A conformance label is a starting point, not proof. A documented report and a task-level check on the workflows students use are what make the claim usable for a decision.

problems.stem: You ask an AI tool to run an accessibility audit on a learning app. It reports 'no accessibility issues found.' What is the defensible interpretation?
options: The tool is fully accessible for all students.
Automated checks catch only some barriers; you still need a task walkthrough with assistive technology and, where possible, disabled-user testing.
The AI result overrides any conformance report.
problems.explanation: Automated audits detect a minority of accessibility barriers. Many barriers only surface in real use with a screen reader, keyboard, or actual disabled testers. The AI result is one input, not a clearance.

problems.stem: An app is accessible and easy to use, but it requires a reliable home internet connection for nightly homework. In an equity analysis, how should a teacher treat this?
options: Ignore it, since the app itself is accessible.
Flag it as an equity risk: a tool that is accessible can still disadvantage students without home connectivity, so the decision must address that gap.
Assume all students have home internet.
Treat connectivity as the vendor's responsibility.
problems.explanation: Accessibility and equity are distinct. A tool can clear accessibility standards yet still impose unequal burdens through its access requirements. A defensible decision names that burden and how it will be addressed.
